questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of a Hyperbola Given its Parametric Equations
questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{5} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{2} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{25} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the hyperbola, we need to eliminate the parameter $t.$ We can do this using the secant-tangent identity.

- Isolating the $\operatorname{sec}⁡t$ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2} & ={sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- Isolating the $\operatorname{tan}⁡t$ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{y}{\sqrt{6}} & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{6})^{2}} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & ={tan}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the two equations into the identity ${tan}^{2}⁡t+1={sec}^{2}⁡t$ and rearranging, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{tan}^{2}⁡t+1 & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{6}+1 & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Parametrizing Part of a Horizontal Hyperbola
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093685/assets/aa1d2d880a575def3e4ca91ac0504ba82fca1ac0908d0fb681bb12e2c81c1081.png)

The quarter-hyperbola above is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a quarter-hyperbola, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093685/assets/ba7e04b9bba38060ab8320365a8b4c88d1dd9f31262ff021ac8b4c65c5d23862.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $[-\pi ,-\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the quarter-hyperbola.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe the required quarter-hyperbola are

$$
x=2\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,-\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equations of a Horizontal Hyperbola Given Graphically
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093685/assets/639d18a8595c082eef85cd22e38b1ae6353b54c259078bf0c15a389ce0ace21f.png)

Find the parametric equations of the hyperbola shown above given that its asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{5}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin with Cartesian equation

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by

$$
x=a\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=b\operatorname{tan}⁡t,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are positive constants.

The vertices of the hyperbola occur at $(\pm a,0).$ From the graph, we have that $(5,0)$ is a vertex of the hyperbola, so $a=5.$

The asymptotes of a horizontal hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{b}{a}x.$ In our case, the asymptotes are $y=\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{5}x,$ and so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{b}{a} & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{5} \\ \frac{b}{5} & =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{5} \\ b & =\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=\sqrt{7}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

One branch of a hyperbola (shown above) is defined by the parametric equations

$$
x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t.
$$

What is the domain of the parameter $t?$

$t\in (${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The parametric equations of the full hyperbola are

$$
x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in [-\pi ,\pi ],\,t\ne \pm \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

To restrict the parameterization to a single branch, we refer to the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093685/assets/c41f14001814c2ab83cc879c35bdaf9166ea9af861fdd216cb382030bc0b047e.png)

We can see that if we restrict $t$ to $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0]$ and $[0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ we get only the right branch.

Therefore, the parametric equations that describe only the right branch are

$$
x=5\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,y=3\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,t\in (-\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{\pi }{2}).
$$
